{"rule": "Return this JSON object with the rule field unchanged and a new passage of about 250 words in the text field.", "text": "The lighthouse went automatic the spring Tomas turned eleven, and his grandfather, who had climbed the hundred and twelve steps every dusk for thirty-one years, was handed a pension letter and a brass plaque with his name spelled wrong. The plaque hung in the kitchen. His grandfather used it to prop open the window when the stove ran hot.

Tomas still climbed the tower most evenings after supper. The door was locked now, but the key had never been collected, and no one seemed to remember it existed. A blinking machine turned the lamp on its own, indifferent and exact, and the old logbooks had been carted off to a museum in the county seat. But his grandfather had taught him to read the sky before the machine arrived, how the gulls flew low ahead of a squall and how the horizon went hard and silver when fog was coming up from the south, and the habit stayed even after the duty had been taken away.

From the gallery he could see the whole bay, the fishing boats coming home in a loose line, the shoals showing pale where the tide pulled back.

One evening in early April a small sailboat tacked toward the harbor mouth, cutting straight across the place where the rocks lay just under the surface at half tide.

Tomas did not shout. He took the old hand lantern from its hook, lit it, and swung it twice toward the north, the way his grandfather had once warned the mackerel crews.

The boat hesitated, then turned wide. Later the sailor rowed ashore and looked up at the tower.

"Who's keeping the light?" he asked.

Tomas thought of the plaque holding open the kitchen window and said, "Someone who used to.""}
